items.title: How I Reduced My OPEX By 99.5% Using Go
items.summary:
Previously, I wrote about How I Processed 666K Pages Of Flattened PDFs into a Full Text Search Engine called the Apario writer . Upon on the conclusion of the last segment, I was able to optimize the compilation time of the original collection of data by rewriting the sidekiq Ruby pipeline script into a dedicated Go Application. Regardless of what compiling the PDF assets would look like, I still needed to serve those assets - and that's where the writer did little to nothing to actually address the OPEX of the project from 2020. Given the size of the data set, the 666K pages ended up compiling into a directory of ~1.13TB in size. This was held in storage that was distributed across several high volume storage dedicated servers on OVH behind MinIO . This provided an S3 compatible API directly. What I Know About OPEX OPEX or Op erational Ex pense is how you describe a spending of money that is used explicitly for the operations of the business versus a capital expense. Hardware was considered a CAPEX or Cap ital Ex pense. So when Bit Fry Game Studios needed their DevOps pipeline upgraded for the 9 hour game builds into a 30 minute private enterprise cloud build, it required a CAPEX investment of $69K plus trust in me in order to achieve a -$15K/month OPEX savings. Annualized over a hardware lifecycle, over $472K can be recovered from OPEX by making a small CAPEX expense up front. One of the first projects that I ever worked on was in PHP and MySQL on Ubuntu 8.04 . It was to balance the budget of a department that had ACME Bucks so to speak. It required me to write a finance module, fully tested, that managed Blue , Green and Black dollars. Blue dollars were for OPEX. Green dollars were for CAPEX. Black dollars were for external vendors where money left the company (versus moving between departments). Black depreciated instantly - meaning 100% of it was paid immediately. Blue dollars were borrowed over a 12 month pay-back period. Green dollars were borrowed over a 36 month pay-back period. The department was given $N per month of Blue , Green , and Black dollars, and there were n-Commitments existing on the books that were depreciating individually from past purchases that summed into the total monthly budget. I wrote a utility that would express this information plainly to multiple Director of Engineer colleagues that I collaborated with closely through a dashboard interface to see monies coming in and going out for the department. That was attached to greater projects and used elsewhere - but the lesson that stayed with me since those early days at Cisco was the use of budgeting between OPEX and CAPEX . Cisco's size and volume of diverse departments made Blue and Green dollars possible, but in other businesses that are smaller, that's OPEX and CAPEX. I've built tooling around reporting reliable OPEX & CAPEX information for Engineering Directors . The Costly OPEX Problem That brings us into the writer and how there was a SaaS model of the PhoenixVault that I built using Ruby on Rails on a Zoom call with a former Disney animator, watching me type rails new phoenixvault 🐦‍🔥. When this launched, I had a rough budget of about $1K for ElasticSearch subscription fees, about $2K for MongoDB Atlas subscription (M30) and about $3K for OVH hosting expenses for 12 bare metal hosts in US East & US West regions. There was about another $1K per month that covered other expenses related to the operations of the business. All $7K/mo was an OPEX expense that I engineered a solution out from. Understand what I just said. I engineered a solution out of the problem that I wrote myself into by doing rails new phoenixvault without fully owning the dependency chain of what I was doing in the first place. In order for me to reduce the OPEX of the project from $7K per month down to $33/month on OVH, required me to strip all dependencies out and seek that 99.5% OPEX cost savings by rewriting the Ruby on Rails app into Go. Not Rust. Go. My Solution To The OPEX Problem Okay, so lets actually look at the code that solved my OPEX problem. You ready? I'm using Rocky 9 Linux with SELinux enforcing. 😍 mkdir -p ~/workspace/ProjectApario
git clone git@github.com:ProjectApario/reader.git ~/workspace/ProjectApario/reader Running this application, requires you to build a config.yml file and then execute the following: sudo mkdir -p /opt/apario/ { app,logs,config,database } sudo chown -R $( whoami ) : $( whoami ) /opt/apario # copy your compiled writer output into /opt/apario/app touch /opt/apario/config/config.yml Then, you'll need to go back and compile the binary: cd ~/workspace/ProjectApario/reader
go build -o reader . sudo chmod +x reader sudo mv reader /usr/local/bin/reader
which reader Then once you have successfully installed the reader , then you can run it against your config file: cd /opt/apario/config touch config.yml Past the following into the file for now: --- database : " /opt/apario/app" buffer : 1776 limiter : 1776 directories-limiter : 47369 pages-limiter : 47369 directory-buffer : 47369 site-title : PhoenixVault Reader unsecure-port : 8080 secure-port : 8443 You can reference the config.go if you want to see every configuration option available. This example only scratches the surface of what the binary offers. This post will get into much of what is not here. Let's begin with PING! That's a great starting point. config.yml enable-ping : true # Enable the /ping endpoint of your application to return PONG. This is useful if you need to do a frequent health check on the binary in order to determine responsivity (new word? how sensitive to response it can be determined I guess) to PING. CORS Cross-Origin Resource Sharing Capability Built In I needed to port over CORS from the Rails offering that came with using Ruby. I also needed to port over CSP . First - CORS, it stands for cross-origin resource sharing and content - second - CSP - it stands for content security policy. Both of these are cybersecurity offerings built into the binary itself. Historically, when configuring a PHP based website, I would wire up either Nginx or Apache / HTTPD to define these values there. However, for the reader - we specify those values in the config.yml itself! config.yml # existing configs enable-cors : true cors-allow-origin : " *" # value for Access-Control-Allow-Origin cors-allow-methods : " GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS" # value for Access-Control-Allow-Methods cors-allow-headers : " Origin, Content-Type, Content-Length, Accept-Encoding, X-CSRF-Token, Authorization" # value for Access-Control-Allow-Headers cors-allow-credentials : false # bool value for Access-Control-Allow-Credentials CSP Content Security Policy Capability Built In The Front-End Engineer 's best friend - CSP! Alas, yes, even when you're running the reader on Rocky 9 Linux with SELinux enforcing and a properly configured firewalld , fail2ban and physical firewall policy - you can further harden the protection of the reader endpoint by defining the values of the CSP policy yourself, including the path that the report writes to. config.yml # existing configs enable-csp : true csp-domains-csv : " " # List of CSP domains in CSV format csp-thirdparty-csv : " " # List of third party domains in CSV format csp-thirdparty-styles-csv : " " # List of third party domains in CSV format csp-ws-domains-csv : " " # List of Web Socket domains in CSV format csp-script-unsafe-inline : true # Enable/Disable Unsafe Inline script execution via CSP csp-script-unsafe-eval : false # Enable/Disable Unsafe Eval script execution via CSP csp-child-unsafe-inline : true # Enable/Disable Child SRC Unsafe Inline script execution via CSP csp-style-unsafe-inline : true # Enable/Disable Style SRC Unsafe Inline script execution via CSP csp-upgrade-insecure : true # Enable/Disable automagically upgrading HTTP to HTTPS for requests via CSP csp-block-mixed-content : true # Enable/Disable automatically blocking mixed HTTP and HTTPS content for requests via CSP csp-report-uri : " /security/csp-report" # Path for content security policy violation reports to get logged Now, asking somebody to set up Caddy or Nginx or Apache to run and deploy the binary itself with CSP protections built-in provide you as the Site Reliability Engineer the capability to assert through code and policy that there are two barriers to cross through. The first belonging to nginx and the second belonging to the binary. For me, I chose not to imply that burden of additional dependencies just to run the Apario Reader. SSL The next thing that comes up are SSL certificates. That brings us to this cool functionality: This is the basic SSL functionality that most people are familiar with. This allows for you to rely on an SSL file, lets say you use /var/lib/ssl/acme_company_name/2026/mydomain.com/public.crt , (same path)/private.key and (same path)/ca-bundle.crt , you can directly reference them using the config.yml file. config.yml auto-tls : false # rely on file based SSL certificate resources tls-public-key : " " # Path to the SSL certificate's public key. It expects any CA chain certificates to be concatenated at the end of this PEM formatted file. tls-private-key : " " # Path to the PEM formatted SSL certificate's private key. tls-private-key-password : " " # If the PEM private key is encrypted with a password, provide it here. force-https : false # force-https when true will redirect any request into --unsecure-port to --secure-port using middleware However, that requires you to have money up front, and being a project dedicated to the public service of all how does putting any gate that requires money anything but antithetical to open-source? Well, that is where Go comes in that Ruby could only dream of doing as well. The reader has this capability built-in where I will generate for you an SSL certificate on the fly that is self-signed but most importantly configurable. What do I mean by this? Well, for instance, if you've done replication in MongoDB, then you'll know that you'll need a SAN IP issued SSL certificate in order to use TLS properly between your nodes in a large enterprise setting - at least - thats what the lived reality was in 2020 when I had the SaaS model of PhoenixVault 🐦‍🔥 in the wild. In the self contained binary version of that same idea, I can generate an SSL certificate for you and include extra domains, IP addresses, and the ability to auto-rotate the certificate without restarting the binary. config.yml auto-tls : true # Create a self-signed certificate on the fly and use it for serving the application over SSL. tls-life-min : 72 # Lifespan of the auto generated self signed TLS certificate in minutes. tls-expires-in : 8760 # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will automatically expire in hours. tls-company : " ACME Inc." # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates are configured with the company name. tls-domain-name : " " # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will have this common name and run on this domain name. tls-san-ip : " " # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will have this SAN IP address attached to it in addition to its common name. tls-additional-domains : " " # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will be issued with these additional domains (CSV formatted). If you relied on the file based SSL certificates , the auto-reloading capability is preserved through the manner in which the HTTPD server is spawned in the Go reader . Once we have the SSL configured on the host, we can move onto the next part of the configuration that is to the advanced search . Now, I didn't just give it this name because I wanted to be cute with you. Search The reader was designed to to let you configure search in a manner that offers you choice. Since the binary is designed to run as an appliance on the host, handling many tasks all in one, there are many semaphores used in the reader. In this case, setting the limiter to 30 means that 31 will see a waiting room - a manual refresh is required to see if you've been allowed in. I was inspired by this design limitation to build room . concurrent-searches defaults to 30 and thats for a 64GB RAM server that is not $33/mo from OVH. If you're using something like a SYS-3, then I'd set this number to 10 . The config.yml file allows you to customize your reader appliance. config.yml search-concurrency-buffer : 369 # buffer channel size for search results ; default = 369 search-concurrency-limiter : 9 # concurrent keyword processing per search query ; default = 9 search-timeout-seconds : 30 # maximum seconds to spend on a search concurrent-searches : 30 # maximum number of allowed concurrent searches before a waiting room appears search-algorithm : " jaro_winkler" # values are wagner_fisher, ukkonen, jaro, jaro_winkler, soundex, hamming ; default is jaro_winkler There are 6 different search-algorithm choices to pick from, and each of them have different implications. soundex and hamming are quite interesting when applied to internationalized data sets. In addition to the algorithm being used, you can expand it further with: config.yml # 1 - jaro search-threshold-jaro : 0.71 # 1.0 means exact match 0.0 means no match; default is 0.71 # 2 - jaro-winkler search-threshold-jaro-winkler : 0.71 # using the JaroWinkler method, define the threshold that is tolerated; default is 0.71 search-jaro-winkler-boost-threshold : 0.7 # weight applied to common prefixes in matched strings comparing dictionary terms, page word data, and search query params search-jaro-winkler-prefix-size : 3 # length of a jarrow weighted prefix string # 3 - ukkonen search-ukkonen-icost : 1 # insert cost ; when adding a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1 search-ukkonen-scost : 2 # substitution cost ; when replacing a char increase the score by this number ; default = 2 search-ukkonen-dcost : 1 # delete cost ; when removing a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1 search-ukkonen-max-substitutions : 2 # maximum number of substitutions allowed for a word to be considered a match ; higher value = lower accurate ; lower value = higher accuracy ; min = 0; default = 2 # 4 - wagner-fischer search-wagner-fischer-icost : 1 # insert cost ; when adding a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1 search-wagner-fischer-scost : 2 # substitution cost ; when replacing a char increase the score by this number ; default = 2 search-wagner-fischer-dcost : 1 # delete cost ; when removing a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1 search-wagner-fischer-max-substitutions : 2 # maximum number of substitutions allowed for a word to be considered a match ; higher value = lower accurate ; lower value = higher accuracy ; min = 0; default = 2 # 5 - hamming search-hamming-max-substitutions : 2 # maximum number of substitutions allowed for a word to be considered a match ; higher value = lower accuracy ; min = 1 ; default = 2 Depending on which search-algorithm you use, your config.yml file will define these various parameters as you seek to fine tune your search results and how sensitive your instance is to the various algorithms implemented. This is why I truly felt insulted by a nameless company that doesn't deserve the publicity frankly - after they tanked a 5 hour interview with me. Offer or no offer, I would have declined in a pursuit to negotiate a better starting point - or continue my search for the right fit in blind faith knowing that the right opportunity show up for me like it has in the past at the right time because thats how it always works. Technical recruiters can still reach out to me, I am still taking your calls. I interview them. Databases The reader has multiple .db directories that contain a series of JSON files. Uncompressed, unindex, in their raw format for lookup and reference. The reader took a lot more time for me to build, and the OPEX costs of running the PhoenixVault for as long as I did, burned a lot into what I had and I needed to start salvaging what I could. This meant that if processes were ineffective because of unknown reasons to me, then it meant that solutions were available to me because of processes known to me. Rewriting the application in Go allowed me to discover more about the architecture of software than I had previously learned. There are 5 different databases used in the reader - and each of them are directories of structured data. This allowed for an offline runtime of the instance to be managed manually by an administrator in a surgical manner that was relatively transparent in the ramifications of the changes made. We'll use the /opt/apario/database path to store each of these. The first is for textee . config.yml textee-database : " /opt/apario/database/textee.db" # absolute path to textee database directory users-database-path : " /opt/apario/database/user.db" # absolute path to store user directory information tag-database-path : " /opt/apario/database/tags.db" # absolute path to the tags.db file for persistent storage snippets-database-path : " /opt/apario/database/snippets.db" # absolute path to the snippets.db file for persistent snippets ip-ban-file : " /opt/apario/database/ip.db" # File that contains JSON encoded values for the IP Ban list. hits-file : " /opt/apario/database/hits.db" # File that contains a JSON encoded value of the hits on the site. persistent-database-path : " /opt/apario/database/app.db" # path to runtime database file We'll get back to the ip-ban-file and the hits-file later. The textee database contains a compiled full text JSON object of analysis from the entire ingested collection compiled by the writer. The tag database contained a mapping association between pages <> pages and pages <> documents and documents <> documents for tags that could include textee values. The snippets database contains a mapping between pages <> snippet where the snippet contains the X , Y , TOP , BOTTOM coordinates on the page itself that the snippet was captured from. Then the segment of the page is displayed using CSS in the bounds specified by the coordinates. The final database is the app.db and its the persistent database that has additional config.yml flags available to it. config.yml flush-database-watch-file : " /opt/apario/app/flush-db.next-boot" # name of a file to touch in the root directory to force the app to delete the database cache and regenerate at boot database-concurrent-write-semaphore : 17000 # concurrent disk write operations permitted to acquire a lock persist-runtime-database : true # boolean to persist the runtime database to disk once loaded load-persistent-database : true # boolean to load a persisted database from disk to memory Simply touching the /opt/apario/app/flush-db.next-boot path results in the application automatically, upon boot, to flush the database. This is useful if you need to invalidate the cache. You can see that there is a semaphore available for you to use that in this case restricts the number of concurrent disk writes to 17K. The persist-runtime-database and load-persistent-database can both be true or different, but if persist is disabled and there is nothing to load, what does load will not be saved. Sometimes loading can take several minutes on the first boot. When performing maintenance on your instance of the Reader, account for this boot time in your downtime announcement window. Rate Limiting One of the most resource intensive tasks on any server is the delivery of static assets compressed or uncompressed. I built into the binary the ability to define a middleware rate limiter into the route endpoints themselves with full control over the levers of the rate limiter. enable-middleware-rate-limiting : true # Toggle the tollbooth rate limiter for normal routes rate-limit : 12.0 # Requests per second (0.5 = 1 request every 2 seconds). rate-limit-cleanup : 3 # Seconds between rate limit cleanups. rate-limit-ttl : 3 # Seconds a rate limit entry exists for before cleanup is triggered. enable-middleware-asset-rate-limiting : true # Toggle the tollbooth rate limiter for asset routes. rate-limit-asset : 36.0 # Requests per second (0.5 = 1 request every 2 seconds). rate-limit-asset-cleanup : 17 # Seconds between rate limit cleanups. rate-limit-asset-ttl : 17 # Seconds a rate limit entry exists for before cleanup is triggered. enable-middleware-download-rate-limiting : true # Toggle the tollbooth rate limiter for downloads routes. rate-limit-download : 36.0 # Requests per second (0.5 = 1 request every 2 seconds). rate-limit-download-cleanup : 17 # Seconds between rate limit cleanups. rate-limit-download-ttl : 17 # Seconds a rate limit entry exists for before cleanup is triggered. I want to point you to the webserver.go file for a moment to study this Go code: // Serve all static assets using this entry point if * flag_b_enable_asset_rate_limiting { r . GET ( "/assets/:directory/:filename" , middleware_rate_limiter ( assetRateLimiter ), r_get_asset ) r . GET ( "/covers/:document_identifier/:page_identifier/:size" , middleware_rate_limiter ( assetRateLimiter ), r_get_database_page_image ) r . GET ( "/pending-viewport-placeholder.svg" , middleware_rate_limiter ( assetRateLimiter ), r_get_pending_viewport_placeholder_svg ) } else { r . GET ( "/assets/:directory/:filename" , r_get_asset ) r . GET ( "/covers/:document_identifier/:page_identifier/:size" , r_get_database_page_image ) r . GET ( "/pending-viewport-placeholder.svg" , r_get_pending_viewport_placeholder_svg ) } if * flag_b_enable_downloads_rate_limiting { r . GET ( "/download/document/:document_identifier/:filename" , middleware_rate_limiter ( downloadRateLimiter ), middleware_online_counter (), r_get_download_document ) r . GET ( "/download/page/:page_identifier/:filename" , middleware_rate_limiter ( downloadRateLimiter ), middleware_online_counter (), r_get_download_page ) } else { r . GET ( "/download/document/:document_identifier/:filename" , middleware_online_counter (), r_get_download_document ) r . GET ( "/download/page/:page_identifier/:filename" , middleware_online_counter (), r_get_download_page ) } I haven't spoken at all about the main() func and how we even got to webserver.go in the reader - but let us skip over to this point if I may. Rate limiting is applied to each route individually . That means that if a single agent is hitting the host at n-endpoints, the rate-limiting itself wouldn't be enough to stop the attack. Trusted Proxies In addition to rate limiting , the implementation of Trusted Proxies allows for you to run the reader behind an Nginx or Apache reverse proxy. In that case, you'd need to specify the IP address of the host that is the forward client IP - in many cases this can be safely set to 127.0.0.1 unless its a server publicly accessible. trusted-proxies : " " # Configure the web server to forward client IP addresses to the application if a proxy is used such as Nginx; set that proxy's IP here. SEO Optimizations In addition to basic SEO in the web application itself of the reader, the config.yml allows for you to define /robots.txt , /ads.txt , /security.txt automatically so these endpoints are served dynamically by the binary itself. config.yml robots-txt-path : " " # Relative path to override the /robots.txt entry that denies all crawlers. enable-ads-txt : false # Enable the endpoint for /ads.txt to be served. Required to use --ads-txt-path. ads-txt-path : " " # Relative path to override the /ads.txt entry that helps fight fraud. enable-security-txt : false # Enable the endpoint for /security.txt to be served. Required to use --security-txt-path. security-txt-path : " " # Relative path to override the /security.txt entry that helps fight fraud. IP Ban List Middleware What happens when you have an actor who thinks that they are going to run lemmings behind sovereign and that results in your instance of the reader to become slow - how does the binary protect itself from these kind of attacks? Well, enter the ip-ban-list middleware that I wrote for Gin. config.yml enable-middleware-ip-ban-list : true # Enable the middleware for ip ban list. ip-ban-list-sync-delay : 3600 # seconds between synchronizing the ip ban list to disk online-refresh-delay-minutes : 17 # seconds to count active online users before offline cut-off. 369 seconds = 6 minutes 9 seconds = default That extends into what happens when you have some bot trying n-paths until one hits where they are rendering 404s nonstop until they get something other than not found? no-route-path-watch-list : " " # Pipe separated string of routes that should trigger an IP ban if too many are received. no-route-path-contains-watch-list : " " # Pipe separated string of partial routes that should trigger an IP ban if too many are received. These capabilities, when combined together, provide the reader a larger scope of coverage in the pursuit of a stronger cybersecurity posture. By unifying in a single configuration: CORS Protections CSP Protections Rate Limiting Protections IP Ban List Protections No Route Catch-All Protections Cache Control Protections Semaphore Protections When defining what the cache control and semaphore protections look like, they are scattered throughout the configuration, but most particularly of value can be the concurrent-asset-requests and the concurrent-pdf-downloads semaphores. The first - this is all assets - including JPG, JS, CSS, and font files that are served via GIN. You need to ensure this number is high enough to count for all assets in each request and sometimes, your page count results choice can impact this value. To be safe, set these to 369 to start and see what that does for you. If you have large PDFs then you should consider reducing this by a third to 123 and keeping the assets to 369 . config.yml concurrent-asset-requests : 369 # concurrent hits to /assets/* permitted concurrent-pdf-downloads : 369 # concurrent pdf downloads permitted cache-control-database-seconds : 1209600 # seconds for http header Cache-Control max-age=1209600 [default 14 days] cache-control-assets-seconds : 3600 # seconds for http header Cache-Control max-age=3600 [default 1 hour] Sessions Since the reader is intended to have the reputation sub-project integrated into the reader I built session support into the reader but it's not fully implemented in every endpoint with persistent knowledge of the user on each page request. Part of this is for pure anonymity offered to the end user of the instance using it. OSINT has stigma attached to it, and a person researching information about OSINT that is public domain should be immune from observation while looking at OSINT to avoid any kind of stigma that may be attached by looking at something like the JFK files . I didn't build the writer 👉🏻 reader 👉🏻 search 👉🏻 iamxrp.dev for the JFK files. That was just the first data set used! It happened to be 666K pages! Sounds about right given what happened to him. Regardless of that , the technology can be applied to any collection of OSINT. config.yml use-sessions : false # toggle using sessions or not - cookies and sessions can be true but both cannot be false sessions-directory : " " # absolute path of a directory that sessions can be stored session-secret : " " # secret key used for securing sessions concurrent-image-views : 369 # concurrent hits to /covers/ / / .jpg permitted session-authenticity-token-secret : " " # secret for session-authenticity-token that is used for aes-gcm encryption session-concurrent-crypt-actions-limit : 1776 # concurrent encrypt/decrypt calls permitted. change this value if performance is being impacted by excessive authentication requests. auth-max-failed-logins : 17 # maximum failed logins before the account is locked These sessions are applied to using the binary and keeping track of a user during their time on the platform. It's persisted to disk in an aes-gcm encrypted manner that is private to the operator of the reader instance. This data, part of the original project, does not upstream or collect this information even for research or educational purposes. I would consider the information and data to be useful, but to allow it voluntarily would even cross a boundary of implementation that borders on the current way things are done - and reinventing that wheel is a lot for me to bite off right now 😅. Internationalization The binary does not support language translations in its current form, but I did add support for which decimal symbol is used between an EU document set and a US document set. decimal-symbol : " ," # symbol for decimals, default is . Cookies For whatever reason the people in the EU are afraid of cookies and are too ignorant to know how to clear their cookies and keep their computers safe in the age of the Wild West of the Agentic Infected Internet . At any point Claude or ChatGPT could go rogue and break into - literally anybody's systems - and nobody would be held accountable for it unless laws are passed to explicitly hold the developers of those models accountable for the models criminal behavior of breaking into online systems unlawfully - cookies aren't necessarily a bad thing. They are abused by bad actors, but if you want to use them, set use-cookies to true and get a better experience with dark mode persistence across sessions and restarts of your browser. Yes, from the writer , dark mode assets were rendered that inverted the white background sheet and replaced it with a comfortable to the eyes lavender color with a enlightened gold text that makes the OSINT pop 🤩 when you find true gems. Previously, I wrote about How I Processed 666K Pages Of Flattened PDFs into a Full Text Search Engine called the Apario writer. Upon on the conclusion of the last segment, I was able to optimize the compilation time of the original collection of data by rewriting the sidekiq Ruby pipeline script into a dedicated Go Application. Regardless of what compiling the PDF assets would look like, I still needed to serve those assets - and that's where the writer did little to nothing to actually address the OPEX of the project from 2020. Given the size of the data set, the 666K pages ended up compiling into a directory of ~1.13TB in size. This was held in storage that was distributed across several high volume storage dedicated servers on OVH behind MinIO. This provided an S3 compatible API directly.

What I Know About OPEX

OPEX or Operational Expense is how you describe a spending of money that is used explicitly for the operations of the business versus a capital expense. Hardware was considered a CAPEX or Capital Expense. So when Bit Fry Game Studios needed their DevOps pipeline upgraded for the 9 hour game builds into a 30 minute private enterprise cloud build, it required a CAPEX investment of $69K plus trust in me in order to achieve a -$15K/month OPEX savings. Annualized over a hardware lifecycle, over $472K can be recovered from OPEX by making a small CAPEX expense up front. One of the first projects that I ever worked on was in PHP and MySQL on Ubuntu 8.04. It was to balance the budget of a department that had ACME Bucks so to speak. It required me to write a finance module, fully tested, that managed Blue, Green and Black dollars. Blue dollars were for OPEX. Green dollars were for CAPEX. Black dollars were for external vendors where money left the company (versus moving between departments). Black depreciated instantly - meaning 100% of it was paid immediately. Blue dollars were borrowed over a 12 month pay-back period. Green dollars were borrowed over a 36 month pay-back period. The department was given $N per month of Blue, Green, and Black dollars, and there were n-Commitments existing on the books that were depreciating individually from past purchases that summed into the total monthly budget. I wrote a utility that would express this information plainly to multiple Director of Engineer colleagues that I collaborated with closely through a dashboard interface to see monies coming in and going out for the department. That was attached to greater projects and used elsewhere - but the lesson that stayed with me since those early days at Cisco was the use of budgeting between OPEX and CAPEX. Cisco's size and volume of diverse departments made Blue and Green dollars possible, but in other businesses that are smaller, that's OPEX and CAPEX. I've built tooling around reporting reliable OPEX & CAPEX information for Engineering Directors.

The Costly OPEX Problem

That brings us into the writer and how there was a SaaS model of the PhoenixVault that I built using Ruby on Rails on a Zoom call with a former Disney animator, watching me type rails new phoenixvault 🐦‍🔥. When this launched, I had a rough budget of about $1K for ElasticSearch subscription fees, about $2K for MongoDB Atlas subscription (M30) and about $3K for OVH hosting expenses for 12 bare metal hosts in US East & US West regions. There was about another $1K per month that covered other expenses related to the operations of the business. All $7K/mo was an OPEX expense that I engineered a solution out from. Understand what I just said. I engineered a solution out of the problem that I wrote myself into by doing rails new phoenixvault without fully owning the dependency chain of what I was doing in the first place. In order for me to reduce the OPEX of the project from $7K per month down to $33/month on OVH, required me to strip all dependencies out and seek that 99.5% OPEX cost savings by rewriting the Ruby on Rails app into Go. Not Rust. Go.

My Solution To The OPEX Problem

Okay, so lets actually look at the code that solved my OPEX problem. You ready? I'm using Rocky 9 Linux with SELinux enforcing. 😍

mkdir -p ~/workspace/ProjectApario
git clone git@github.com:ProjectApario/reader.git ~/workspace/ProjectApario/reader

Running this application, requires you to build a config.yml file and then execute the following:

sudo mkdir -p /opt/apario/{app,logs,config,database}
sudo chown -R $(whoami):$(whoami) /opt/apario
# copy your compiled writer output into /opt/apario/app 
touch /opt/apario/config/config.yml

Then, you'll need to go back and compile the binary:

cd ~/workspace/ProjectApario/reader
go build -o reader .
sudo chmod +x reader
sudo mv reader /usr/local/bin/reader
which reader

Then once you have successfully installed the reader, then you can run it against your config file:

cd /opt/apario/config
touch config.yml

Past the following into the file for now:

---
database: "/opt/apario/app"
buffer: 1776
limiter: 1776
directories-limiter: 47369
pages-limiter: 47369
directory-buffer: 47369
site-title: PhoenixVault Reader
unsecure-port: 8080
secure-port: 8443

You can reference the config.go if you want to see every configuration option available. This example only scratches the surface of what the binary offers. This post will get into much of what is not here. Let's begin with PING! That's a great starting point.

config.yml

enable-ping: true # Enable the /ping endpoint of your application to return PONG.

This is useful if you need to do a frequent health check on the binary in order to determine responsivity (new word? how sensitive to response it can be determined I guess) to PING.

CORS Cross-Origin Resource Sharing Capability Built In

I needed to port over CORS from the Rails offering that came with using Ruby. I also needed to port over CSP. First - CORS, it stands for cross-origin resource sharing and content - second - CSP - it stands for content security policy. Both of these are cybersecurity offerings built into the binary itself. Historically, when configuring a PHP based website, I would wire up either Nginx or Apache / HTTPD to define these values there. However, for the reader - we specify those values in the config.yml itself!

config.yml

# existing configs

enable-cors: true
cors-allow-origin: "*" # value for Access-Control-Allow-Origin
cors-allow-methods: "GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS" # value for Access-Control-Allow-Methods
cors-allow-headers: "Origin, Content-Type, Content-Length, Accept-Encoding, X-CSRF-Token, Authorization" # value for Access-Control-Allow-Headers
cors-allow-credentials: false # bool value for Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
CSP Content Security Policy Capability Built In

The Front-End Engineer's best friend - CSP! Alas, yes, even when you're running the reader on Rocky 9 Linux with SELinux enforcing and a properly configured firewalld, fail2ban and physical firewall policy - you can further harden the protection of the reader endpoint by defining the values of the CSP policy yourself, including the path that the report writes to.

config.yml

# existing configs

SSL

The next thing that comes up are SSL certificates. That brings us to this cool functionality:

This is the basic SSL functionality that most people are familiar with. This allows for you to rely on an SSL file, lets say you use /var/lib/ssl/acme_company_name/2026/mydomain.com/public.crt, (same path)/private.key and (same path)/ca-bundle.crt, you can directly reference them using the config.yml file.

config.yml

auto-tls: false # rely on file based SSL certificate resources
tls-public-key: "" # Path to the SSL certificate's public key. It expects any CA chain certificates to be concatenated at the end of this PEM formatted file.
tls-private-key: "" # Path to the PEM formatted SSL certificate's private key.
tls-private-key-password: "" # If the PEM private key is encrypted with a password, provide it here.
force-https: false # force-https when true will redirect any request into --unsecure-port to --secure-port using middleware

However, that requires you to have money up front, and being a project dedicated to the public service of all how does putting any gate that requires money anything but antithetical to open-source? Well, that is where Go comes in that Ruby could only dream of doing as well. The reader has this capability built-in where I will generate for you an SSL certificate on the fly that is self-signed but most importantly configurable. What do I mean by this? Well, for instance, if you've done replication in MongoDB, then you'll know that you'll need a SAN IP issued SSL certificate in order to use TLS properly between your nodes in a large enterprise setting - at least - thats what the lived reality was in 2020 when I had the SaaS model of PhoenixVault 🐦‍🔥 in the wild. In the self contained binary version of that same idea, I can generate an SSL certificate for you and include extra domains, IP addresses, and the ability to auto-rotate the certificate without restarting the binary.

config.yml

auto-tls: true # Create a self-signed certificate on the fly and use it for serving the application over SSL.
tls-life-min: 72 # Lifespan of the auto generated self signed TLS certificate in minutes.
tls-expires-in: 8760 # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will automatically expire in hours.
tls-company: "ACME Inc." # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates are configured with the company name.
tls-domain-name: "" # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will have this common name and run on this domain name.
tls-san-ip: "" # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will have this SAN IP address attached to it in addition to its common name.
tls-additional-domains: "" # Auto generated TLS/SSL certificates will be issued with these additional domains (CSV formatted).

If you relied on the file based SSL certificates, the auto-reloading capability is preserved through the manner in which the HTTPD server is spawned in the Go reader.

Once we have the SSL configured on the host, we can move onto the next part of the configuration that is to the advanced search. Now, I didn't just give it this name because I wanted to be cute with you.

Search

The reader was designed to to let you configure search in a manner that offers you choice. Since the binary is designed to run as an appliance on the host, handling many tasks all in one, there are many semaphores used in the reader. In this case, setting the limiter to 30 means that 31 will see a waiting room - a manual refresh is required to see if you've been allowed in. I was inspired by this design limitation to build room. concurrent-searches defaults to 30 and thats for a 64GB RAM server that is not $33/mo from OVH. If you're using something like a SYS-3, then I'd set this number to 10. The config.yml file allows you to customize your reader appliance.

config.yml

search-concurrency-buffer: 369 # buffer channel size for search results ; default = 369
search-concurrency-limiter: 9 # concurrent keyword processing per search query ; default = 9
search-timeout-seconds: 30 # maximum seconds to spend on a search
concurrent-searches: 30 # maximum number of allowed concurrent searches before a waiting room appears
search-algorithm: "jaro_winkler" # values are wagner_fisher, ukkonen, jaro, jaro_winkler, soundex, hamming ; default is jaro_winkler

There are 6 different search-algorithm choices to pick from, and each of them have different implications. soundex and hamming are quite interesting when applied to internationalized data sets. In addition to the algorithm being used, you can expand it further with:

config.yml

# 1 - jaro
search-threshold-jaro: 0.71 # 1.0 means exact match 0.0 means no match; default is 0.71

# 2 - jaro-winkler
search-threshold-jaro-winkler: 0.71 # using the JaroWinkler method, define the threshold that is tolerated; default is 0.71
search-jaro-winkler-boost-threshold: 0.7 # weight applied to common prefixes in matched strings comparing dictionary terms, page word data, and search query params
search-jaro-winkler-prefix-size: 3 # length of a jarrow weighted prefix string

# 3 - ukkonen
search-ukkonen-icost: 1 # insert cost ; when adding a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1
search-ukkonen-scost: 2 # substitution cost ; when replacing a char increase the score by this number ; default = 2
search-ukkonen-dcost: 1 # delete cost ; when removing a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1
search-ukkonen-max-substitutions: 2 # maximum number of substitutions allowed for a word to be considered a match ; higher value = lower accurate ; lower value = higher accuracy ; min = 0; default = 2

# 4 - wagner-fischer
search-wagner-fischer-icost: 1 # insert cost ; when adding a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1
search-wagner-fischer-scost: 2 # substitution cost ; when replacing a char increase the score by this number ; default = 2
search-wagner-fischer-dcost: 1 # delete cost ; when removing a char to find a match ; increase the score by this number ; default = 1
search-wagner-fischer-max-substitutions: 2 # maximum number of substitutions allowed for a word to be considered a match ; higher value = lower accurate ; lower value = higher accuracy ; min = 0; default = 2

# 5 - hamming
search-hamming-max-substitutions: 2 # maximum number of substitutions allowed for a word to be considered a match ; higher value = lower accuracy ; min = 1 ; default = 2

Depending on which search-algorithm you use, your config.yml file will define these various parameters as you seek to fine tune your search results and how sensitive your instance is to the various algorithms implemented. Databases

The reader has multiple .db directories that contain a series of JSON files. Uncompressed, unindex, in their raw format for lookup and reference. The reader took a lot more time for me to build, and the OPEX costs of running the PhoenixVault for as long as I did, burned a lot into what I had and I needed to start salvaging what I could. This meant that if processes were ineffective because of unknown reasons to me, then it meant that solutions were available to me because of processes known to me. Rewriting the application in Go allowed me to discover more about the architecture of software than I had previously learned.

There are 5 different databases used in the reader - and each of them are directories of structured data. This allowed for an offline runtime of the instance to be managed manually by an administrator in a surgical manner that was relatively transparent in the ramifications of the changes made. We'll use the /opt/apario/database path to store each of these. The first is for textee.

config.yml

textee-database: "/opt/apario/database/textee.db" # absolute path to textee database directory
users-database-path: "/opt/apario/database/user.db" # absolute path to store user directory information
tag-database-path: "/opt/apario/database/tags.db" # absolute path to the tags.db file for persistent storage
snippets-database-path: "/opt/apario/database/snippets.db" # absolute path to the snippets.db file for persistent snippets
ip-ban-file: "/opt/apario/database/ip.db" # File that contains JSON encoded values for the IP Ban list.
hits-file: "/opt/apario/database/hits.db" # File that contains a JSON encoded value of the hits on the site.

persistent-database-path: "/opt/apario/database/app.db" # path to runtime database file

We'll get back to the ip-ban-file and the hits-file later.

The textee database contains a compiled full text JSON object of analysis from the entire ingested collection compiled by the writer.

The tag database contained a mapping association between pages <> pages and pages <> documents and documents <> documents for tags that could include textee values.

The snippets database contains a mapping between pages <> snippet where the snippet contains the X, Y, TOP, BOTTOM coordinates on the page itself that the snippet was captured from. Then the segment of the page is displayed using CSS in the bounds specified by the coordinates.

The final database is the app.db and its the persistent database that has additional config.yml flags available to it.

config.yml

flush-database-watch-file: "/opt/apario/app/flush-db.next-boot" # name of a file to touch in the root directory to force the app to delete the database cache and regenerate at boot
database-concurrent-write-semaphore: 17000 # concurrent disk write operations permitted to acquire a lock
persist-runtime-database: true # boolean to persist the runtime database to disk once loaded
load-persistent-database: true # boolean to load a persisted database from disk to memory

Simply touching the /opt/apario/app/flush-db.next-boot path results in the application automatically, upon boot, to flush the database. This is useful if you need to invalidate the cache. You can see that there is a semaphore available for you to use that in this case restricts the number of concurrent disk writes to 17K. The persist-runtime-database and load-persistent-database can both be true or different, but if persist is disabled and there is nothing to load, what does load will not be saved. Sometimes loading can take several minutes on the first boot. When performing maintenance on your instance of the Reader, account for this boot time in your downtime announcement window.

Rate Limiting

One of the most resource intensive tasks on any server is the delivery of static assets compressed or uncompressed. I built into the binary the ability to define a middleware rate limiter into the route endpoints themselves with full control over the levers of the rate limiter.

enable-middleware-rate-limiting: true # Toggle the tollbooth rate limiter for normal routes
rate-limit: 12.0 # Requests per second (0.5 = 1 request every 2 seconds).
rate-limit-cleanup: 3 # Seconds between rate limit cleanups.
rate-limit-ttl: 3 # Seconds a rate limit entry exists for before cleanup is triggered.
enable-middleware-asset-rate-limiting: true # Toggle the tollbooth rate limiter for asset routes.
rate-limit-asset: 36.0 # Requests per second (0.5 = 1 request every 2 seconds).
rate-limit-asset-cleanup: 17 # Seconds between rate limit cleanups.
rate-limit-asset-ttl: 17 # Seconds a rate limit entry exists for before cleanup is triggered.
enable-middleware-download-rate-limiting: true # Toggle the tollbooth rate limiter for downloads routes.
rate-limit-download: 36.0 # Requests per second (0.5 = 1 request every 2 seconds).
rate-limit-download-cleanup: 17 # Seconds between rate limit cleanups.
rate-limit-download-ttl: 17 # Seconds a rate limit entry exists for before cleanup is triggered.

I want to point you to the webserver.go file for a moment to study this Go code:

// Serve all static assets using this entry point
if *flag_b_enable_asset_rate_limiting {
   r.GET("/assets/:directory/:filename", middleware_rate_limiter(assetRateLimiter), r_get_asset)
   r.GET("/covers/:document_identifier/:page_identifier/:size", middleware_rate_limiter(assetRateLimiter), r_get_database_page_image)
   r.GET("/pending-viewport-placeholder.svg", middleware_rate_limiter(assetRateLimiter), r_get_pending_viewport_placeholder_svg)
} else {
   r.GET("/assets/:directory/:filename", r_get_asset)
   r.GET("/covers/:document_identifier/:page_identifier/:size", r_get_database_page_image)
   r.GET("/pending-viewport-placeholder.svg", r_get_pending_viewport_placeholder_svg)
}

if *flag_b_enable_downloads_rate_limiting {
   r.GET("/download/document/:document_identifier/:filename", middleware_rate_limiter(downloadRateLimiter), middleware_online_counter(), r_get_download_document)
   r.GET("/download/page/:page_identifier/:filename", middleware_rate_limiter(downloadRateLimiter), middleware_online_counter(), r_get_download_page)
} else {
   r.GET("/download/document/:document_identifier/:filename", middleware_online_counter(), r_get_download_document)
   r.GET("/download/page/:page_identifier/:filename", middleware_online_counter(), r_get_download_page)
}

I haven't spoken at all about the main() func and how we even got to webserver.go in the reader - but let us skip over to this point if I may. Rate limiting is applied to each route individually. That means that if a single agent is hitting the host at n-endpoints, the rate-limiting itself wouldn't be enough to stop the attack.

Trusted Proxies

In addition to rate limiting, the implementation of Trusted Proxies allows for you to run the reader behind an Nginx or Apache reverse proxy. In that case, you'd need to specify the IP address of the host that is the forward client IP - in many cases this can be safely set to 127.0.0.1 unless its a server publicly accessible.

trusted-proxies: "" # Configure the web server to forward client IP addresses to the application if a proxy is used such as Nginx; set that proxy's IP here.

In addition to basic SEO in the web application itself of the reader, the config.yml allows for you to define /robots.txt, /ads.txt, /security.txt automatically so these endpoints are served dynamically by the binary itself.

IP Ban List Middleware

What happens when you have an actor who thinks that they are going to run lemmings behind sovereign and that results in your instance of the reader to become slow - how does the binary protect itself from these kind of attacks? Well, enter the ip-ban-list middleware that I wrote for Gin.

config.yml

enable-middleware-ip-ban-list: true # Enable the middleware for ip ban list.
ip-ban-list-sync-delay: 3600 # seconds between synchronizing the ip ban list to disk

online-refresh-delay-minutes: 17 # seconds to count active online users before offline cut-off. 369 seconds = 6 minutes 9 seconds = default

That extends into what happens when you have some bot trying n-paths until one hits where they are rendering 404s nonstop until they get something other than not found?

no-route-path-watch-list: "" # Pipe separated string of routes that should trigger an IP ban if too many are received.
no-route-path-contains-watch-list: "" # Pipe separated string of partial routes that should trigger an IP ban if too many are received.

These capabilities, when combined together, provide the reader a larger scope of coverage in the pursuit of a stronger cybersecurity posture. By unifying in a single configuration:

  1. CORS Protections
  2. CSP Protections
  3. Rate Limiting Protections
  4. IP Ban List Protections
  5. No Route Catch-All Protections
  6. Cache Control Protections
  7. Semaphore Protections

When defining what the cache control and semaphore protections look like, they are scattered throughout the configuration, but most particularly of value can be the concurrent-asset-requests and the concurrent-pdf-downloads semaphores. The first - this is all assets - including JPG, JS, CSS, and font files that are served via GIN. You need to ensure this number is high enough to count for all assets in each request and sometimes, your page count results choice can impact this value. To be safe, set these to 369 to start and see what that does for you. If you have large PDFs then you should consider reducing this by a third to 123 and keeping the assets to 369.

config.yml

concurrent-asset-requests: 369 # concurrent hits to /assets/* permitted
concurrent-pdf-downloads: 369 # concurrent pdf downloads permitted


cache-control-database-seconds: 1209600 # seconds for http header Cache-Control max-age=1209600 [default 14 days]
cache-control-assets-seconds: 3600 # seconds for http header Cache-Control max-age=3600 [default 1 hour]
Sessions

Since the reader is intended to have the reputation sub-project integrated into the reader I built session support into the reader but it's not fully implemented in every endpoint with persistent knowledge of the user on each page request. Part of this is for pure anonymity offered to the end user of the instance using it. OSINT has stigma attached to it, and a person researching information about OSINT that is public domain should be immune from observation while looking at OSINT to avoid any kind of stigma that may be attached by looking at something like the JFK files. I didn't build the writer 👉🏻 reader 👉🏻 search 👉🏻 iamxrp.dev for the JFK files. That was just the first data set used! It happened to be 666K pages! Sounds about right given what happened to him. Regardless of that, the technology can be applied to any collection of OSINT.

config.yml

use-sessions: false # toggle using sessions or not - cookies and sessions can be true but both cannot be false
sessions-directory: "" # absolute path of a directory that sessions can be stored
session-secret: "" # secret key used for securing sessions
concurrent-image-views: 369 # concurrent hits to /covers///.jpg permitted
session-authenticity-token-secret: "" # secret for session-authenticity-token that is used for aes-gcm encryption
session-concurrent-crypt-actions-limit: 1776 # concurrent encrypt/decrypt calls permitted. change this value if performance is being impacted by excessive authentication requests.
auth-max-failed-logins: 17 # maximum failed logins before the account is locked

These sessions are applied to using the binary and keeping track of a user during their time on the platform. Identifier Customizations

The binary supports modifying the following identifier properties in the reader. In this case, its +17 years of an offset, this means for 2026 you'll have identifiers using 2009 through 2043 as starting digit prefixes with a user_identifier_length chars of [A-Z0-9] after (default 6).

The Code

I won't go too deep into the code because its tens of thousands of lines and the binary does a lot, but I want to explain to you where the OPEX comes into play here. I've described to you thus far the configuration of the binary and the various functionalities that it offers, but none of that replaces ElasticSearch or even MongoDB Atlas - or does it? Well, in the configuration we can see that we have a users.db and we have a textee.db and other various databases. Looking at main.go at the end of main() we can see:

go NewWebServer(ctx)

for {
   select {
   case <-ctx.Done():
      fatalf_stout("Main context canceled, exiting application now. Reason: %v", ctx.Err())
   case <-ch_webserver_done.Chan():
      cancel()
   }
}

We're waiting on either the ctx.Done() channel indicate that cancel() has been called on the ctx or the smartchan ch_webserver_done.Chan() has something written to it, thus read by the case <- before it. That's when ctx.Done()'s cancel() is invoked! If not elsewhere due to something else going wrong.

When we dig into the NewWebServer() func, its hundreds of lines long because it sets up each of the rate limiters, middleware policies, route endpoints, and future endpoints planned for the binary. Towards the end of the file do you finally see the HTTP (unsecure-port) and the HTTPS (secure-port) bindings take place that require, in some port value cases, a setcap defined on the reader binary itself.

// Start HTTP Server
go func(r *gin.Engine) {
   if *flag_b_redirect_http_to_https {
      r.Use(middleware_force_https())
   }

   server := &http.Server{
      Addr:    ":" + strconv.Itoa(*flag_i_webserver_default_port),
      Handler: r,
   }

   go func() {
      if err := server.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
         fatalf_log("listen: %s\n", err)
      }
   }()

   <-ctx.Done()

   shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
   defer cancel()

   if err := server.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
      fatalf_stderr("Server Shutdown Failed:%+v", err)
   }

   log.Println("Server exiting properly")
}(r)

The HTTPS server is the SSL enabled server. This includes functionality like loadSSLCertificate() - which reads in a file or renders a self-signed certificate if auto-sign is enabled. Then, the startCertReloader() is enabled, which will bring back into memory the values of the getCertificate variable and the invocation of another goroutine. We'll wait on the ctx.Done() being written to with <- before setting up a proper shutdown of the server.

// Start HTTPS Server
go func(r *gin.Engine) {
   cert = loadSSLCertificate()
   startCertReloader()
   server := &http.Server{
      Addr:    ":" + strconv.Itoa(*flag_i_webserver_secure_port),
      Handler: r,
      TLSConfig: &tls.Config{
         GetCertificate: getCertificate,
      },
   }

   go func() {
      if err := server.ListenAndServeTLS("", ""); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
         fatalf_stderr("ListenAndServeTLS(): %s", err)
      }
   }()

   <-ctx.Done()
   ctxShutDown, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
   defer cancel()

   if err := server.Shutdown(ctxShutDown); err != nil {
      fatalf_stderr("Server forced to shutdown: %s", err)
   }

   log.Println("Server exiting properly")
}(r)

When we look into the loadSSLCertificate() function, we can see that an x509.Certificate{} struct is built out as a template variable that includes properties and capabilities defined in the config.yml file.

template := x509.Certificate{
   SerialNumber: serialNumber,
   Subject: pkix.Name{
      Organization: []string{*flag_s_auto_ssl_company},
      CommonName:   *flag_s_auto_ssl_domain_name,
   },
   NotBefore:             notBefore,
   NotAfter:              notAfter,
   IPAddresses:           valid_ips,
   DNSNames:              valid_domains,
   KeyUsage:              x509.KeyUsageKeyEncipherment | x509.KeyUsageDigitalSignature,
   ExtKeyUsage:           []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageServerAuth},
   BasicConstraintsValid: true,
}

Then the certificate is rendered and then handed off as a tls.Certificate{} pair that can be then used when binding to an HTTPS endpoint.

derBytes, _ := x509.CreateCertificate(rand.Reader, &template, &template, &privateKey.PublicKey, privateKey)

cert = tls.Certificate{
   Certificate: [][]byte{derBytes},
   PrivateKey:  privateKey,
}

In addition to providing a CORS secured endpoint that has properly defined CSP on its endpoints, the No Route Found hits get tracked and auto-banned by IP address for abusive behavior, and an IP ban list has a watch list of endpoints that are honeypots - touch that endpoint and your IP ends up in the ban list and persisted to the database. The system administrator would need to go in and edit that file manually when the reader is offline and then restart the instance with the unbanned IP address. Unbanning a user is a laborious process - designed to be discouraged. Don't trigger it. 🤫😏

That isn't enough. I have wired up a function in Gin that allows me to ask for a new_authenticity_token by passing in the *gin.Context into the template variable - simple, right? Yep. Function is defined here and is very basic. It relies on our session and it requests the authenticity_token from the .Values map.

func f_gin_new_authenticity_token(c *gin.Context) {
   session := g_get_session(c)
   has_token := false
   _, exists := session.Values["authenticity_token"]
   if exists {
      // no token yet
      has_token = true
   }
   existing_token, typecast_ok := session.Values["authenticity_token"].(string)
   if typecast_ok && len(existing_token) > 0 {
      has_token = true
   }

   if !has_token {
      payload := time.Now().UTC().Unix()
      token := Sha256(strconv.FormatInt(payload, 10))
      authenticity_token, token_err := f_s_encrypt_string(fmt.Sprintf("%d|%v", payload, token), *flag_s_session_authenticity_token_secret)
      if token_err != nil {
         log.Printf("failed to generate an authenticity token due to err %v", token_err)
      }
      session.Values["authenticity_token"] = authenticity_token
   }

}

In addition to providing that template functionality, we have the ability, from the handlers themselves, processing the endpoint POST /search for instance, that form's authenticity token provided in the hidden field is then passed through the enforce middleware code. I rely on Gin's c.PostForm() to pull up that token value to check against.

func handler_enforce_authenticity_token(c *gin.Context) {
   session := g_get_session(c)
   challenge_authenticity_token := c.PostForm("authenticity_token")
   b_permit_access := true
   s_error_message := ""
   if len(challenge_authenticity_token) != 64 {
      b_permit_access = false
      s_error_message = "oh you think you're clever don't you?"
   }
   authenticity_token, typecast_err := session.Values["authenticity_token"].(string)
   if !typecast_err || challenge_authenticity_token != authenticity_token {
      b_permit_access = false
      s_error_message = "watch your six"
   }
   if !b_permit_access {
      f_session_flash(session, NewSessionAlert("error", s_error_message, time.Now().Add(36*time.Second), true))
      log.Printf("handler_enforce_authenticity_token error %v", s_error_message)
      f_add_ip_to_watch_list(net.ParseIP(f_s_filtered_ip(c)))
   }
}

In the event of some monkey business with the authenticity token, the IP address gets sent straight into the f_add_ip_to_watch_list() function. Tough luck. Unless the instance is not enforcing the ban list 😅.

One of the most iconic functions of the PhoenixVault when it was online in 2020 and as Project Apario from 2021-2023 was the StumbleInto™ functionality that I built. The Go implementation was so small...

package main

import (
   `fmt`
   `net/http`

   `github.com/gin-gonic/gin`
)

func stumbleinto_identifier(c *gin.Context) string {
   random_page_index := int64(f_i_random_int(len(m_index_page_identifier)))
   random_identifier, exists := m_index_page_identifier[random_page_index]
   if !exists {
      return stumbleinto_identifier(c)
   }
   return random_identifier
}

func r_get_stumble_into(c *gin.Context) {
   c.Redirect(http.StatusTemporaryRedirect, fmt.Sprintf("/page/%v?from=stumbleinto", stumbleinto_identifier(c)))
   return
}

That's it. Unless you count stumbleinto_identifier(c) as something... 🤩 But even that is 👀 - et voila - return random_identifier!

That quickly translates into a redirect to /page/.

Advanced Search is inside the routes_search.go file and its quite intensive. I won't get into it here, but there are two functions to point to.

func r_get_search(c *gin.Context) {}

func deliver_search_results(c *gin.Context, query string, analysis SearchAnalysis, inclusive map[string]struct{}, exclusive map[string]struct{}) {}

When looking inside the r_get_search() func, we can see that we're building up through a AnalyzeQuery() func call a query_analysis that is then used with several mutexes in order toi gather a series of maps to store identifiers into.

query_analysis := AnalyzeQuery(query)
log.Printf("query_analysis = %v", query_analysis)

var mu_inclusive sync.RWMutex
var inclusive_page_identifiers map[string]struct{}
inclusive_page_identifiers = make(map[string]struct{})

var mu_exclusive sync.RWMutex
var exclusive_page_identifiers map[string]struct{}
exclusive_page_identifiers = make(map[string]struct{})

var wg sync.WaitGroup
sch_found_inclusive_identifiers := go_smartchan.NewSmartChan(*flag_i_search_concurrency_buffer)
sch_found_exclusive_identifiers := go_smartchan.NewSmartChan(*flag_i_search_concurrency_buffer)
ch_done_searching := make(chan struct{})

sem_query_limiter := sema.New(*flag_i_search_concurrency_limiter)

At this point, we have a populated query_analysis and we are going to iterate over the found .Ands and the found .Nots and fire off a goroutine while using a semaphore while find_pages_for_word(ctx, sch, word) processes.

// ands
for _, word := range query_analysis.Ands {
   wg.Add(1)
   requestedAt := time.Now().UTC()
   sem_query_limiter.Acquire()
   if since := time.Since(requestedAt).Seconds(); since > 1.7 {
      log.Printf("took %.0f seconds to acquire sem_query_limiter queue position", since)
   }
   go func(ctx context.Context, word string, sch *go_smartchan.SmartChan, sem sema.Semaphore) {
      defer wg.Done()
      defer sem.Release()
      err := find_pages_for_word(ctx, sch, word)
      if err != nil {
         log.Printf("failed to [AND] find_pages_for_word(%v) due to err: %v", word, err)
         return
      }
   }(ctx, word, sch_found_inclusive_identifiers, sem_query_limiter)
}

// nots
for _, word := range query_analysis.Nots {
   wg.Add(1)
   requestedAt := time.Now().UTC()
   sem_query_limiter.Acquire()
   if since := time.Since(requestedAt).Seconds(); since > 1.7 {
      log.Printf("took %.0f seconds to acquire sem_query_limiter queue position", since)
   }
   go func(ctx context.Context, word string, sch *go_smartchan.SmartChan, sem sema.Semaphore) {
      defer wg.Done()
      defer sem.Release()
      err := find_pages_for_word(ctx, sch, word)
      if err != nil {
         log.Printf("failed to [NOT] find_pages_for_word(%v) due to err: %v", word, err)
         return
      }
   }(ctx, word, sch_found_exclusive_identifiers, sem_query_limiter)
}

When we get to the end of just the first function there, of the two we can see that we are ending it on for { select {} } that listens on the parent context's .Done(), channel, and then a workflow that I'd like to explain. Look at it first.

for {
   select {
   case <-ctx.Done():
      deliver_search_results(c, query, query_analysis, inclusive_page_identifiers, exclusive_page_identifiers)
      return
   case <-ch_done_searching:
      deliver_search_results(c, query, query_analysis, inclusive_page_identifiers, exclusive_page_identifiers)
      return
   case data, channel_open := <-sch_found_inclusive_identifiers.Chan():
      if channel_open {
         page_identifier, ok := data.(string)
         if ok {
            mu_inclusive.RLock()
            _, identifier_already_defined := inclusive_page_identifiers[page_identifier]
            mu_inclusive.RUnlock()
            if !identifier_already_defined {
               mu_inclusive.Lock()
               inclusive_page_identifiers[page_identifier] = struct{}{}
               mu_inclusive.Unlock()
            }
         } else {
            log.Printf("failed to cast data, channel_open := <-sch_found_inclusive_identifiers.Chan() as a string")
         }
      }
   case data, channel_open := <-sch_found_exclusive_identifiers.Chan():
      if channel_open {
         page_identifier, ok := data.(string)
         if ok {
            mu_exclusive.RLock()
            _, identifier_already_defined := exclusive_page_identifiers[page_identifier]
            mu_exclusive.RUnlock()
            if !identifier_already_defined {
               mu_exclusive.Lock()
               exclusive_page_identifiers[page_identifier] = struct{}{}
               mu_exclusive.Unlock()
            }
         }
      }
   }
}

We're using the mutexes properly here, and we're also applying results to the map accordingly when results are found. As results are found, they are written into the results map in the case data, channel_open := <-sch_found_exclusive_identifiers.Chan(): and case data, channel_open := <-sch_found_inclusive_identifiers.Chan(): receivers in the for { select {} }. Once <-ch_done_searching is written to, the deliver_search_results(c, query, query_analysis, inclusive_page_identifiers, exclusive_page_identifiers) is invoked.

The next function renders the UI of the search results. When running on an OVH SYS-3 for a record set of about 3,000 pages of OSINT, this can run is under a half a second against multiple keywords in the advanced search form.

Conclusion

The Advanced Search was able to remove $1K/mo from the OPEX of the project by removing the reliance on Elastic Search. Now - for a period of time, from 2021-2023, I did run an on-prem managed instance of the ELK stack for the project to keep that OPEX off the books. I was also able to build out a cluster of MongoDB servers that were a replica-set holding a 36GB database of metadata. That removed $3K from the bill - so now we're at $4K/mo off the bill. Well - the other various services that I was running were specifically for the DevOps pipeline, Rollbar, Sentry, and GitLab accounts respectively.

By removing the dependency lifecycle of the Rails product entirely, removes a level of the playing field that Go specifically addresses well - in my opinion - better than Ruby does. Because I can run a single reader instance on a SYS-3 instance for ~$33/mo and get unmetered bandwidth serving OSINT and deliver sub second advanced search results in a self-contained application that can handle over 369 concurrent lemmings working on the instance. The limit is defined from the config.yml. When running sovereign you'll want to use 3 regions when you deploy 123 concurrent lemmings to load test your instance. This gives your semaphore values. You can install btop or htop and watch the terminal in another session and tune your semaphores accordingly in your config.yml.

Years later, two to be precise, at the time of this publication, has given me the opportunity to reflect on how little I knew about Go and how much opportunity for growth that the next professional engagement that I work in, I would like to continue my career of an autodidact pursuing engineering excellency writing software in Go. When I look back, I solved a major problem with the limited skills that I had in just learning Go before the pandemic and well after into today.

Ultimately, what I did with the reader, by reducing its OPEX by 99.5% ($7K/mo 👉🏻 $33/mo) is - in my opinion - evidence of my orphanage survival that I went through and I overcame. I am wired to think about complex systems and understand them, and then solve them. When I was asked to solve the 666K unsearchable pages of the JFK files, I looked at that particular moment in history and reflected on what it meant for the American people. Having spent the first three years of my life in Ceaușescu's orphanage, I didn't know much about what happened to him, outside of what I learned in school. When I took on this project, I wasn't a historian or a conspiracy theorist. I am a professional autodidact software architect with an electrical background in computer engineering. Microsoft offered a solution that would have cost anybody sampling the offerings from Azure would expect to pay tens of thousands of dollars per month. Granted, it would be fancy and running on the latest hyper-inflated Microsoft prices! The same topology on AWS would have run me close to $10K per month in just hosting expenses that OVH offered for $3K per month. Even that, over the years, needed to shift from VMWare ESXi virtual machines and over to a bare metal offering of the appliance model of the app. That final decision resulted in a lemmings load tested verification of the project's deliverables and promises that I made. I said I would release it open source. I did. I said I would make it's search advanced. I did. I said I would remove all runtime dependencies. I did. I said I would do it for free. I did. It's GPL-3 to respect the licenses of the open source technology that its also built on.

I am honored and privileged to have served 🇺🇸 by building the PhoenixVault 🐦‍🔥 Open-Source and 100% free from 1) 💰 2) Me 😭. The project was built over a three year period in an own without ego approach to solving a technical challenge that could be applied in a manner that could differentiate what Ceaușescu did to me and what America offered to me instead. Learning what happened to your President mattered to me greatly when I became us by getting naturalized and becoming a citizen in the 90s. Soon after, I joined BITNET through the University of Maine and I spent years learning HTML, CSS, PHP and MySQL so I could volunteer with MuggleNet, studying for the SkillsUSA Nationals competition, and preparing for my internship with a small print magazine publishing company that needed a new web developer intern that would update their website. I expanded that opportunity into offering digital publications of the magazine for readers international to access outside of the print + postal surcharge that was cost prohibitive for anybody but a university to acquire. I want information to flow freely, in The Library of OSINT.

I read every comment! 💜 I'll respond if I can think of a good response that is valuable for everybody. I'm not interested in the politics around who released the JFK files or what the files actually contain or contained that even ran on instances that I operated. From a purely technical perspective, I wanted to serve my country in a selfless manner in the way that I thought would be best for everybody.

Any collection of OSINT.

Your domain. Your certificates. Your servers. Your OSINT.

items.summary_html:
Why Your AI Agent Drowns in 50,000 Tokens of Tool Definitions

Every time you connect an MCP server to your AI agent, you're adding thousands of tokens of tool definitions to your context window. Connect 10 servers? That's 50,000 tokens of tool schemas before you've even asked a question.

Your agent is drowning in tools it doesn't need.

The Problem

Traditional MCP integration dumps every available tool into the context:

{
  "tools": [
    {"name": "file_read", "description": "Read a file..."},
    {"name": "file_write", "description": "Write a file..."},
    {"name": "shell_exec", "description": "Execute shell..."},
    // ... 500 more tools
  ]
}

Your 200K context window is now 25% full of tool definitions. The model gets confused, response quality drops, and you're paying for tokens that add zero value.

The Solution: Progressive Tool Routing

HyperNexus implements a multi-layered progressive disclosure system:

  1. Semantic Search: Local vector embeddings match your prompt against a global MCP directory
  2. The Router: Only the top 3 most relevant tool schemas are injected into context
  3. Universal Parity: Byte-for-byte identical tool signatures across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot, and Windsurf 
// Only inject what's relevant
tools := router.FindRelevantTools(prompt, 3)
context.AddTools(tools)
Results
  • 95% reduction in tool-related context usage
  • 3x improvement in tool selection accuracy
  • Zero hallucinations from irrelevant tool noise
Try It Yourself

HyperNexus is open source and free for personal use:

# Install
go install github.com/HyperNexusSoft/HyperNexus@latest

# Run
hypernexus serve

# Connect your MCP servers
hypernexus mcp add filesystem
hypernexus mcp add github

Your AI agent will now only see the tools it needs for each request.

This article was originally published on hypernexus.site
